name: Anxiety Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

aeo.what_is: Anxiety symptoms directly caused by a medical condition's physiological effects, not from psychological stress about illness.

description.overview: A clinically significant anxiety disturbance directly attributable to the physiological effects of another medical condition, not better explained by another mental disorder. The anxiety may manifest as generalized anxiety, panic attacks, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, or phobic avoidance.

what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.title: The Unexpected Storm
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.story: Marcus, 52, prided himself on staying calm under pressure as a logistics manager. Then he started waking at 3 AM with his heart racing, drenched in sweat, convinced something terrible was about to happen. His wife urged him to see their doctor, who ran tests and discovered his thyroid was severely overactive. Within weeks of starting thyroid medication, the nightly panic attacks subsided—but Marcus still felt shaken by how a medical problem could hijack his emotions so completely.

what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.title: The Breathing Room
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.story: Elena, 67, had managed her COPD for years with medications and careful pacing. But lately, any small exertion left her gasping, and the fear of not being able to breathe became overwhelming. She stopped going to her book club, then to the grocery store. Her doctor adjusted her respiratory medications and referred her to a therapist specializing in health anxiety. Elena learned that her anxiety was both a response to her worsening breathing and made worse by the low oxygen levels—her body and mind were caught in a feedback loop.

what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.title: The Silent Signal
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.story: After recovering from a minor stroke at age 58, David found himself constantly on edge, startling at sounds and unable to relax. His neurologist explained that the stroke had affected areas of his brain involved in regulating anxiety. David felt frustrated—he'd expected physical rehabilitation, not this invisible struggle with fear. His care team added an SSRI and cognitive therapy to his recovery plan, and gradually the background hum of dread began to fade.

what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.title: The Sugar Rollercoaster
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.story: Priya, 29, was diagnosed with diabetes in college and managed it well for years. But recently, her anxiety spikes coincided with episodes of shaky hands and racing thoughts—signs her blood sugar was dropping too low. Her endocrinologist adjusted her insulin regimen, and Priya started checking her glucose before assuming every anxious moment was 'just stress.' Understanding the physical trigger helped her distinguish medical urgency from emotional worry.

what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.title: The Heart's Messenger
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life.story: At 45, James noticed his heart would suddenly race and pound, leaving him breathless and terrified he was having a heart attack. After his third ER visit, a cardiologist identified an arrhythmia—his heart's electrical system was misfiring. The panic James felt was real, but it was triggered by the physical sensation of his irregular heartbeat. A medication to control the arrhythmia helped, and so did learning techniques to manage the fear response when his heart skipped a beat.

common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Relief that symptoms have a medical explanation, not 'just in my head'
Frustration about needing treatment for both the medical condition and anxiety
Confusion about whether anxiety is causing physical symptoms or vice versa
Worry that managing anxiety means ignoring real medical warning signs
Validation that the emotional struggle is connected to physical health
Concern about adding psychiatric medication to an already complex medical regimen

content.temporal_criteria: No specific duration required; diagnosis based on temporal relationship between medical condition onset/course and anxiety symptoms, plus evidence from history, examination, or laboratory findings that anxiety is direct physiological consequence of the medical condition.
content.misdiagnosis_explained: This diagnosis is missed when providers attribute all anxiety to 'stress about being sick' without investigating whether the medical condition itself (hyperthyroidism, heart arrhythmia, COPD) is directly causing anxiety through physiological mechanisms. It's over-diagnosed when normal worry about a serious illness is mislabeled as pathological, or when an adjustment disorder is incorrectly attributed to direct physiological effects rather than psychological response to illness.
content.diagnostic_criteria: A. Prominent anxiety, panic attacks, obsessions/compulsions predominate. B. Evidence from history, exam, or labs that the disturbance is the direct pathophysiological consequence of another medical condition. C. Not better explained by another mental disorder. D. Not occurring exclusively during delirium. E. Causes clinically significant distress or impairment.
content.prevalence: Varies depending on medical condition; common in endocrine, cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological disorders.
content.age_of_onset: Any age, depending on onset of underlying medical condition.
content.neurobiology: Anxiety may arise from structural brain changes (e.g., stroke, tumor), neurotransmitter imbalances (e.g., altered serotonin, norepinephrine, GABA), inflammatory cytokines, dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, or autonomic hyperactivity. Conditions such as hyperthyroidism can increase adrenergic activity, while hypoglycemia activates sympathetic arousal.

history: Detailed onset and temporal relationship between anxiety symptoms and medical illness.
Medication review for agents that may exacerbate anxiety (e.g., corticosteroids, stimulants).
physical_exam: Full medical exam focused on systems relevant to suspected cause.
Neurological exam for focal deficits or signs of CNS pathology.
laboratory_tests: Neuroimaging for CNS lesions or structural abnormalities.

common_associated_medical_conditions: Cardiovascular: Arrhythmias, congestive heart failure, myocardial infarction.
Neurological: Stroke, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, temporal lobe epilepsy.

core: Excessive fear or anxiety temporally related to medical condition onset.
Panic attacks in absence of typical triggers.

biological: CNS lesions or chronic neurological disease.
environmental: Chronic stress from medical treatment demands.

impact_on_life.work: Missed work due to both medical and anxiety symptoms.
impact_on_life.school: Difficulty focusing; avoidance of attendance due to health fears.
impact_on_life.social: Withdrawal from activities due to medical fragility or anxiety.

primary: Optimal treatment of underlying medical condition.
Address any iatrogenic contributors (e.g., medication changes).
psychotherapy: Psychoeducation about the medical condition to reduce uncertainty.
medications: SSRIs (e.g., sertraline, escitalopram) for persistent anxiety.
SNRIs (e.g., venlafaxine XR) if comorbid pain.
Short-term benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam, clonazepam) for acute severe anxiety, with caution in respiratory compromise or CNS disease.
care_coordination: Close collaboration between mental health, primary care, and specialty providers.

treatment_goals: Reduce anxiety symptoms and functional impairment.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Attributing all anxiety symptoms to a primary psychiatric disorder without assessing medical triggers.
Failure to review medications that may cause anxiety.
overdiagnosis_factors: Attributing normal anxiety responses to serious illness as pathological.
Mislabeling adjustment disorder with anxiety as a direct physiological effect.

specifiers.with_panic_attacks: Meets criteria for panic attacks linked to medical condition.
specifiers.with_generalized_anxiety: Predominantly GAD-like symptoms linked to medical condition.

warning_signs: Sudden onset of severe anxiety in older adults or those without psychiatric history.
Anxiety accompanied by neurological or cardiovascular symptoms.
self_help_strategies: Education about the medical condition to reduce uncertainty.
Stress management techniques compatible with physical limitations.
Support groups for individuals with the same medical illness.

childhood: School refusal or somatic complaints triggered by illness-related anxiety.
adolescence: Fear of symptom recurrence interfering with social or academic activities.
adulthood: Avoidance of activities due to fear of exacerbating illness symptoms.
older_adults: Heightened anxiety about health changes; overlap with cognitive decline concerns.

first_person_statements: I thought I was losing my mind—turns out my thyroid was the culprit. Once we got that under control, the constant panic finally lifted.
My doctor kept saying my anxiety was making my breathing worse, but it felt like my breathing was making my anxiety worse. They were both right.
After my stroke, I couldn't understand why I felt so afraid all the time. Learning it was part of the brain injury actually helped me be patient with recovery.
The hardest part was figuring out when to check my blood sugar versus when to use my anxiety coping skills. Sometimes it was both.
I felt angry that treating my heart condition wasn't enough—I had to deal with the emotional fallout too. But addressing both made all the difference.

real_life_examples.title: The Thyroid Trap
real_life_examples.story: Rachel, a 44-year-old teacher, began experiencing unexplained panic attacks during quiet moments—grading papers at home, waiting in line at the grocery store. She'd always been calm and steady, so the sudden waves of terror confused her. Her primary care doctor noticed her resting heart rate was 110 and ordered thyroid tests. Hyperthyroidism was flooding her system with excess thyroid hormone, triggering her sympathetic nervous system into overdrive. After starting medication to reduce thyroid activity, Rachel's panic attacks became less frequent. However, months of living in fear had created a secondary layer of anticipatory anxiety. She worked with a therapist on CBT to address the lingering 'what if it happens again' worry while her endocrinologist continued to adjust her thyroid medication. Rachel learned to distinguish between physiological arousal from her thyroid and anxious thoughts—a skill that helped her feel more in control even as her body healed.

real_life_examples.title: The Breathless Spiral
real_life_examples.story: Tom, 71, had lived with COPD for over a decade. He knew how to pace himself, use his inhaler, and recognize when to call his pulmonologist. But over six months, his anxiety about breathlessness escalated to the point where he avoided leaving his apartment. Even thinking about walking to the mailbox triggered a sensation of air hunger. His doctor ran pulmonary function tests and found his lung capacity had indeed declined—but not enough to explain the severity of his avoidance. Tom was caught in a cycle: his worsening COPD made breathing harder, which triggered anxiety, which made him breathe shallowly and rapidly, which worsened his sense of suffocation. His care team started him on a long-acting bronchodilator and referred him to pulmonary rehabilitation, where he learned breathing techniques to manage both the physical and emotional components of dyspnea. A low-dose SSRI helped reduce the hair-trigger anxiety response. Slowly, Tom rebuilt his confidence, first walking to the mailbox, then around the block, learning that he could tolerate discomfort without catastrophe.

real_life_examples.title: The Stroke's Shadow
real_life_examples.story: After a small stroke at age 60, Linda expected physical therapy for her weakened left arm. What she didn't expect was the overwhelming anxiety that arrived two weeks later. She startled at every sound, felt a constant sense of dread, and couldn't sleep. Her neurologist explained that the stroke had affected areas involved in emotional regulation—her brain's 'alarm system' was stuck in overdrive due to the injury. Linda felt betrayed by her own mind. She started an SSRI and began working with a neuropsychologist who specialized in stroke recovery. Therapy helped her understand that her anxiety wasn't a character flaw or a sign of weakness—it was a direct consequence of brain damage. She learned grounding techniques and gradually her nervous system recalibrated. A year later, most of the anxiety had resolved, though she remained more sensitive to stress than before the stroke. Linda joined a stroke support group and found comfort in sharing this 'invisible' aspect of stroke recovery with others who understood.

real_life_examples.title: The Heart That Lied
real_life_examples.story: James, a 49-year-old accountant, visited the ER three times in two months, convinced he was having a heart attack. Each time, tests showed no heart damage—but they did reveal frequent episodes of rapid, irregular heartbeat. A cardiologist diagnosed an arrhythmia: James's heart would suddenly race or skip beats, triggering a flood of adrenaline and panic. The physical sensation was real, and so was the fear it provoked. James started a medication to control his heart rhythm and began CBT for panic disorder. In therapy, he learned that while his arrhythmia triggered the initial physical sensation, his catastrophic interpretation ('I'm dying') amplified his distress. He practiced noticing his heartbeat without judgment, reminding himself that an irregular beat was uncomfortable but not dangerous. Over time, the medication reduced the frequency of arrhythmias, and James's fear response diminished. He still felt anxious when his heart skipped, but he no longer spiraled into full-blown panic.

comparisons.condition_a: Anxiety Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition
comparisons.explanation: Both involve excessive anxiety, but in anxiety due to a medical condition, symptoms are directly caused by physiological changes from the illness (e.g., hyperthyroidism increasing heart rate and arousal). In GAD, anxiety is chronic, pervasive worry about multiple life domains without a clear medical cause. Timing is key: medical-induced anxiety closely follows the onset or worsening of the medical condition and often improves with treatment of that condition.

comparisons.condition_a: Anxiety Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition
comparisons.explanation: Adjustment disorder involves emotional distress in response to a stressor (like receiving a serious medical diagnosis), but it's a psychological reaction, not a direct physiological effect. Anxiety due to a medical condition results from the body's biological response to the illness itself—for example, low oxygen from COPD triggering panic, not just worry about having COPD. Someone can have both: psychological distress about being ill and anxiety directly caused by the illness's physical effects.

comparisons.condition_a: Anxiety Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition
comparisons.explanation: Both are secondary anxiety disorders caused by something other than a primary psychiatric condition. The key difference is the source: medical-condition-induced anxiety comes from illnesses like hyperthyroidism or stroke, while substance/medication-induced anxiety is triggered by drugs, alcohol, or medications (including those used to treat medical conditions). There can be overlap—for instance, corticosteroids prescribed for an autoimmune disease can cause anxiety, making it substance-induced rather than medical-condition-induced.

faqs.question: How do you know if anxiety is caused by a medical condition versus just stress about being sick?
faqs.answer: Timing and physiology are key clues. If anxiety symptoms start closely after a medical condition begins or worsens, and medical tests show physiological changes that can directly cause anxiety (like elevated thyroid hormones, low oxygen, or brain lesions), it's likely medical-condition-induced. Stress about being sick typically doesn't improve when the medical condition is treated, whereas physiologically-driven anxiety often does. Your doctor will also look for patterns—does anxiety spike with disease flares and improve with disease control?

faqs.question: Can treating my medical condition alone fix the anxiety?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, yes—especially if caught early. If hyperthyroidism is controlled or an arrhythmia is corrected, anxiety may resolve completely. However, many people develop secondary anxiety patterns (fear of symptoms returning, avoidance behaviors) that persist even after the medical issue is managed. In those cases, therapy (like CBT) and sometimes anxiety medication can help address the psychological aftermath.

faqs.question: Should I see a psychiatrist or my medical doctor for this?
faqs.answer: Ideally, both, working together. Your medical doctor or specialist should manage the underlying condition (thyroid disorder, heart problem, etc.), while a psychiatrist or therapist can help with anxiety symptoms through medication and therapy. Integrated care—where your providers communicate—leads to the best outcomes because both the physical and emotional aspects need attention.

faqs.question: Will I need to take psychiatric medication forever?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. If the medical condition is successfully treated and stabilized, anxiety often decreases and medication can eventually be tapered. However, some chronic medical conditions (like COPD or Parkinson's disease) continue to cause physiological anxiety, and ongoing medication may help. The decision to continue or stop is made collaboratively with your doctors based on symptom patterns and quality of life.

faqs.question: Is this anxiety real, or is it just my imagination?
faqs.answer: It's absolutely real. When a medical condition disrupts your body's chemistry or brain function, the anxiety you feel is a genuine physiological response—not something you're making up or could simply 'think away.' That said, how you interpret and respond to those sensations can influence how much distress you experience, which is why therapy can help even when the root cause is physical.

faqs.question: Can this diagnosis lead to more anxiety about my health?
faqs.answer: It's a valid concern. Some people find it reassuring to know their anxiety has a medical explanation, while others worry about their body being 'broken' in yet another way. Psychoeducation—learning how your specific condition affects anxiety—can reduce fear of the unknown. Understanding the link between your body and mind often helps you feel more in control, not less.

faqs.question: What if my doctor doesn't believe my anxiety is related to my medical condition?
faqs.answer: Bring up the timing: when did anxiety start relative to your medical diagnosis or symptom changes? Share specific examples of how anxiety worsens with disease flares. Ask for a referral to a specialist (endocrinologist, neurologist, cardiologist) who can assess whether your condition is known to cause anxiety. You can also request consultation with a psychiatrist experienced in medical-psychiatric interfaces—these specialists are trained to identify when medical and mental health issues overlap.

faqs.question: Can children get anxiety from medical conditions?
faqs.answer: Yes. Children with conditions like hyperthyroidism, diabetes with frequent low blood sugar, or asthma can experience anxiety as a direct result of physiological changes. Young children may not be able to articulate anxious feelings, so they might show irritability, clinginess, or behavioral changes instead. Pediatricians and child psychiatrists work together to distinguish medical causes from primary anxiety.

faqs.question: Are panic attacks always a sign of anxiety disorder, or could they be medical?
faqs.answer: Panic attacks can be triggered by many medical conditions—arrhythmias, hyperthyroidism, hypoglycemia, pheochromocytoma (adrenal tumor), or even asthma attacks. If panic attacks appear suddenly in someone without prior anxiety history, especially alongside physical symptoms like heart palpitations, sweating, or tremor, a medical workup is essential. It's important to rule out medical causes before assuming it's a primary panic disorder.

faqs.question: What's the difference between anxiety due to a medical condition and panic disorder?
faqs.answer: In panic disorder, panic attacks occur unexpectedly without a clear trigger, and there's no identifiable medical cause—it's a primary psychiatric condition. In anxiety due to a medical condition, panic-like symptoms are directly triggered by a physiological process (e.g., hyperthyroidism, low blood sugar, heart arrhythmia). The key is evidence of a medical condition that can produce anxiety, and a temporal link between the medical issue and anxiety onset.

faqs.question: Can anxiety due to a medical condition vs. generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) be distinguished?
faqs.answer: Yes. GAD involves chronic, excessive worry about multiple everyday concerns (work, relationships, health, finances) that's hard to control and persists regardless of life circumstances. Anxiety due to a medical condition is tied to the onset and course of a specific illness—it often improves when the illness is treated and worsens when the illness flares. Lab tests, imaging, and medical exams can identify physiological causes in medical-condition-induced anxiety, whereas GAD has no such findings.

faqs.question: How is anxiety disorder due to a medical condition different from adjustment disorder with anxiety?
faqs.answer: Adjustment disorder is a psychological response to a stressor (like being diagnosed with a serious illness)—it's about emotional difficulty coping with the situation. Anxiety due to a medical condition is caused by the direct physiological effects of the illness itself (e.g., altered hormones, oxygen levels, brain chemistry). You could have both: struggle emotionally with your diagnosis (adjustment disorder) and experience anxiety as a biological consequence of the disease process.

faqs.question: Anxiety disorder due to a medical condition vs. substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder—what's the difference?
faqs.answer: Both are secondary anxiety disorders, meaning something other than a primary mental health condition is the cause. Medical-condition-induced anxiety comes from illnesses like hyperthyroidism, COPD, or stroke. Substance/medication-induced anxiety is caused by drugs, alcohol, or medications (even those prescribed for medical conditions, like corticosteroids). The line can blur: if a medication for your medical condition causes anxiety, it's substance-induced, not medical-condition-induced.

faqs.question: Can you have anxiety disorder due to a medical condition and another anxiety disorder at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, it's possible. Someone with a longstanding history of generalized anxiety disorder could develop additional anxiety symptoms directly caused by a new medical condition like hyperthyroidism. In such cases, treating the medical condition may reduce some anxiety, but the underlying GAD would still require ongoing management. Clinicians assess the timeline and symptom patterns to determine if one or both diagnoses apply.

faqs.question: Does everyone with a medical condition that can cause anxiety actually develop this disorder?
faqs.answer: No. Many people with hyperthyroidism, COPD, or heart disease don't develop clinically significant anxiety. Individual differences in brain chemistry, genetics, stress resilience, and prior mental health history all play a role. Some people experience mild nervousness that doesn't interfere with functioning, while others develop severe, impairing anxiety requiring treatment. The diagnosis is only made when anxiety is prominent, distressing, and clearly linked to the medical condition.

faqs.question: If I have chronic illness, will I always have anxiety?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. With proper treatment of the underlying condition, many people see significant improvement in anxiety. Even with chronic, incurable illnesses, anxiety can be managed through medication adjustments, therapy, lifestyle changes, and learning to cope with physical symptoms. Over time, many people adapt and find their anxiety becomes less intense or easier to manage, even if the medical condition persists.

faqs.question: What should I do if my anxiety gets worse even though my medical condition is being treated?
faqs.answer: Tell your medical and mental health providers right away. Worsening anxiety despite medical treatment could mean: (1) the medical treatment needs adjustment, (2) you've developed a secondary, independent anxiety disorder, (3) there's a new medical issue, or (4) medication side effects are contributing. Don't wait—persistent anxiety deserves evaluation and intervention, whether that's medication changes, therapy, or both.

content.when_to_seek_help: When anxiety is intense, persistent, and directly related to a medical condition, leading to avoidance or inability to follow treatment plans.

positive_factors: Access to integrated medical and mental health care.
challenging_factors: Limited insight into the anxiety-medical link.
